blocks.html: We describe Rukha, a counterfactual narrative engine that takes a foundational text, decomposes it into a causal event graph, perturbs load-bearing nodes via Pearl’s do-calculus, and propagates coherent counterfactual trajectories forward through the graph using the Abduction–Action–Prediction algorithm. Unlike prior counterfactual story-generation systems, which operate at depth one against a single original, Rukha operates recursively to depths five and six: a perturbation downstream of a previous perturbation produces a counterfactual-of-a-counterfactual, and so on. Our central claim is that recursive depth, properly scaffolded, is computationally tractable where unscaffolded long-form generation collapses. Three convergences make it so. First, formal: Pearl’s framework, Lewis–Ryan possible-worlds narratology, the Aaronson–Watrous pspace characterization of multiverse computation, and the 5D Brainfuck mtt esolang all describe the same structure — a directed acyclic graph of branching states governed by coherence constraints. Second, structural: persistent data structures with structural sharing (hash array mapped tries, Merkle-dags, zero-suppressed decision diagrams) reduce the O(bdˆ) apparent state space to storage proportional to actual divergence between universes. Third, architectural: explicit causal dags scaffold what unscaffolded chain-of-thought cannot — recent work documents reasoning-horizon decay at of chain length and near-random performance on nested counterfactuals without external structure. We demonstrate the system on the Book of Jonah, whose 16 consensus events and quantified chiastic symmetry — the 39-Hebrew-word parallel between Jonah 4:2–3 and 4:10–11, machine-verifiable against the Westminster Leningrad Codex — make it the optimal minimal test case. We close by arguing that Rukha is best understood as a computational midrash engine: a 2,000-year scholarly tradition of generating textual counterfactuals as interpretive practice, made recursive and explicit. The output is not a dataset of alternate endings but a topology of grace.
Introduction: A Story Is a Graph of Forks

Current language models are trained on what humans wrote. This limitation is rarely named but it is severe. The corpus of human storytelling is the surviving trajectory of a much larger possibility space — every story we did not tell, every ending the author cut, every counterfactual the redactor smoothed. A model trained only on the surviving trajectory inherits the survivor bias. It learns what stories are but not what they could have been, and consequently it learns narrative causation only as a shadow on the wall of narrative outcome.

Rukha is a proposal to lift the shadow. The system takes a foundational text — the Book of Jonah, the Mahābhārata, the Iliad, the Brothers Karamazov — decomposes it into a causal event graph using constrained-decoding event extraction, identifies which nodes carry the graph’s structural load, perturbs those nodes through Pearl’s do-calculus, and propagates coherent alternative trajectories forward via the Abduction–Action–Prediction (aap) algorithm. The output is a corpus of causally-coherent alternate histories: not random mutations, not GPT-fabulations, but lawful trajectories through the narrative-physics established by the source material.

What distinguishes Rukha from prior work in counterfactual story generation is depth. TimeTravel [47], educat [10], the pasta dataset [33], and the broader counterfactual-rewriting literature [44] all operate at depth one: a single “what if” applied to a single original story. Rukha operates recursively. A perturbation downstream of a previous perturbation produces a counterfactual-of-a-counterfactual; that, in turn, can be perturbed again. We aim for depth five and six.

This is not a marginal extension of prior work. It is the regime where counterfactual reasoning becomes interesting — and the regime where unscaffolded language-model generation has been shown to fail. Recent empirical work documents a Reasoning Horizon at roughly of chain length, beyond which intermediate reasoning tokens have negative effect on the final output [12]. Other work documents Shallow Lock-in and Deep Decay as characteristic failure modes of long-chain reasoning [45]. counterbench [5], a 2025 benchmark for counterfactual reasoning in language models, finds that leading models perform near-randomly on its Nested subset — the condition closest to Rukha’s regime. Rukha’s bet is that this collapse is not fundamental; it is a consequence of asking models to perform recursive counterfactual reasoning without external scaffolding. Given an explicit causal graph, persistent state, and the Abduction–Action–Prediction protocol enforced by constrained decoding, the bet is that recursive depth becomes tractable.
What This Paper Argues
The paper makes four claims and defends each.

items: Formal equivalence. Pearl’s structural causal models, David Lewis’s possible-worlds semantics, Marie-Laure Ryan’s textual actual world plus modal satellite worlds, and the multiverse-time-travel primitives of the 5D Brainfuck mtt esolang all describe the same underlying structure: a directed acyclic graph of branching states governed by coherence constraints. Rukha is the operationalization of this structure.

Complexity tractability. Recursive counterfactual propagation on causal event graphs lives within pspace, by Aaronson–Watrous [1]. Persistent data structures with structural sharing — hash array mapped tries [2], Merkle-dags as in Git and ipfs, and zero-suppressed decision diagrams [21] — reduce apparent O(bdˆ) storage to storage proportional to the actual divergence between universes.

Recursion depth is the empirical frontier. No published system has demonstrated coherent counterfactual reasoning at depth five or six on natural-language narrative. The literature has named the problem (counterbench-Nested, the Reasoning Horizon, Shallow Lock-in / Deep Decay) but not solved it. This is Rukha’s contribution.

Sacred narrative is the optimal demonstration target. The Book of Jonah, with its 48 verses, 16 consensus events, and quantified chiastic structure — the 39-Hebrew-word parallel between Jonah 4:2–3 and 4:10–11, machine-verifiable against the Westminster Leningrad Codex — is the smallest text where Rukha’s claims can be rigorously demonstrated. The theological theme of the book — the disorientation of receiving mercy you did not think the recipient deserved — becomes computational under perturbation.

blocks.html: Foundations
Pearl’s Do-Calculus and the AAP Algorithm

A structural causal model (scm) over variables V={V_1,…,V_n} specifies, for each V_i, a structural equation V_i=f_i(pa(V_i),U_i) where pa(V_i) are the causal parents of V_i and U_i is exogenous noise. The do-operator do(V_i:=v′) surgically replaces f_i with the constant assignment V_i=v′, severing all incoming edges to V_i while leaving downstream structural equations intact. This is Pearl’s central technical move [34]: an intervention is structural surgery, not conditioning.
Counterfactual reasoning in this framework follows the Abduction–Action–Prediction algorithm [35,36]:

items: Abduction. Given the observed facts E (the evidence encoded in the actual textual world), update the prior over exogenous noise: P(U)↦P(U∣E). In narrative terms, abduction infers the latent assumptions about characters, settings, and world-rules that are compatible with what we read.
Action. Apply the intervention: do(V_i:=v′). The structural equation for V_i is replaced; incoming edges are severed.
Prediction. Forward-propagate the modified scm in topological order. For each downstream node V_j, compute V_j=f_j(pa(V_j),U_j) using the updated P(U∣E) and the modified parent values.

blocks.html: In Rukha, each step is performed by a 70B-parameter language model under xgrammar-constrained json decoding [50]. The structural equations f_j are not closed-form functions; they are prompts. The model is asked, given the observed narrative and a perturbation at V_i, to predict the new value of V_j in a manner consistent with the perturbed graph and the abducted exogenous priors. The grammar constrains the output schema — event id, type, agents, location, verse-reference — so that hallucination of structure is impossible at the syntactic level. What remains is the semantic problem: did the model abduct correctly, did it propagate correctly, did it preserve coherence?
Recursion: The Pearl–Robins Decomposition

Sequential interventions in acyclic scms decompose cleanly. This is the foundational result for nested counterfactuals: Pearl and Robins [36] establish that compound interventions in dags with hidden variables can be evaluated as a chain of single-step do-operations, each conditioned on the consequences of those preceding it. Correa, Lee, and Bareinboim [6] extend this to nested counterfactual identification from arbitrary surrogate experiments, providing a sound and complete algorithm for the identifiability question.

The implication: a depth-N recursive counterfactual is mathematically well-defined whenever the underlying graph is acyclic and the identification conditions are satisfied. Rukha’s narrative graphs are acyclic by construction — causal edges flow forward in narrative time — and the identification conditions are trivially satisfied because all events are observable. There is no hidden-variable confounding in a fixed text: the text is the data.

blocks.label: Proposition — Recursive AAP Decomposition
blocks.html: Let G=(V,E) be an acyclic narrative event graph and let (v_i1​,v′_i1​),…,(v_iN​,v′_iN​) be a sequence of perturbations such that v_ik​ is reachable from v_ik−1​ in G for all k>1. Then the depth-N recursive counterfactual G(N)ˆ​ is the result of applying aap sequentially: G(0)ˆ​=G; G(k)ˆ​=AAP(G(k−1)ˆ​,v_ik​↦v′_ik​). The decomposition is well-defined and unique up to the abduction distribution at each step.

What this proposition does not guarantee is that the language-model implementation of aap is faithful to the abduction distribution at each step. It does not guarantee that depth five or six is computationally achievable in practice. These are the empirical questions the paper later confronts.
Possible-Worlds Narratology
Rukha’s perturbations are not statistical; they are semantic. The language for talking about narrative possibility is narratology, specifically Marie-Laure Ryan’s possible-worlds theory [41].

Ryan distinguishes the textual actual world (taw) — what is presented as factual within the fiction — from the satellite worlds of characters: their knowledge worlds (what they believe), wish worlds (what they want), obligation worlds (what they should do), intention worlds (what they plan to do). Each character is a center of multiple modal worlds, and narrative tension arises when the satellite worlds of one character conflict with the taw or with the satellite worlds of another.

Lewis [22] grounds counterfactual reasoning in similarity orderings over possible worlds: the counterfactual “if A had not happened, B would not have happened” is true if and only if in the closest possible world where A does not happen, B does not either. Ryan adapts Lewis’s framework to fiction via the principle of minimal departure: readers reconstrue the fictional world as the closest possible to the actual world, deviating only where the text forces deviation.

These two frameworks — Pearl’s scm and Ryan-Lewis modal worlds — describe the same object from two angles. Pearl asks: what happens if I surgically modify this node? Lewis asks: what is the closest world where the modification holds? In an acyclic narrative dag with no hidden confounders, the answers coincide: the aap-propagated counterfactual is the closest possible world.
Complexity: Why pspace?

The ceiling of Rukha’s computational regime is established by Aaronson and Watrous [1]: classical and quantum computation in the presence of closed timelike curves under Deutsch’s self-consistency condition is exactly pspace-complete. Their result formalizes a long folkloric intuition: time-travel computation, properly constrained, is no more powerful than polynomial space.

Rukha is not implementing closed timelike curves. Its counterfactual trajectories propagate forward; they do not loop back. But the ambient class within which Rukha operates — bounded-depth multiverse exploration with consistency constraints — is a strict subset of pspace, and Aaronson and Watrous’s result anchors the upper bound.

The 5D Brainfuck With Multiverse Time Travel esolang [14] provides an engineering-folkloric instantiation of the same idea: a programming language whose primitives include spawning parallel timelines, killing pointers across timelines, and rewinding within timelines. The esolang is, deliberately, a minimal model of pspace-class multiverse computation. Rukha can be read as the narrative-domain instantiation of the same primitives: spawn-timeline = perturbation, kill-pointer = quality filtering, rewind = re-abduction.
The Recursion-Depth Claim
Why Depth Matters

Counterfactual reasoning at depth one is well-trodden territory. TimeTravel [47] provides 29,849 supervised single-step counterfactual rewrites of rocstories narratives; educat [10] achieves unsupervised single-step rewriting via causal-effect estimation. The pasta dataset [33] introduces participant-state perturbations as a cleaner formalism. None of these systems propagates recursively. Each “what if” is applied to the canonical original; counterfactuals do not stack.

The reason this matters is that depth is where narrative physics becomes visible. At depth one, a perturbation reveals the immediate causal neighbors of an event. At depth three, perturbations reveal which patterns survive when the structural scaffolding is repeatedly disturbed. At depth five and six, an empirical question becomes testable: do generated counterfactual variants cluster into narrative archetypes, or do they spread uniformly through possibility space? The answer to this question is the difference between narrative being a soft topology with attractor basins (Propp’s functions, Campbell’s monomyth, Hogan’s prototypical structures, Reagan’s six emotional arcs [40]) and narrative being an arbitrary high-dimensional space.

If narrative has attractor basins, then deep counterfactual exploration should reveal them: most depth-six variants of Jonah should land in a small number of recurrent shapes, regardless of which specific nodes were perturbed. If narrative lacks attractor basins, then depth-six variants should fan out and not return. Either result is publishable. The first vindicates Propp, Campbell, and Hogan as empirical claims about narrative cognition; the second falsifies them.
The Empirical Landscape
What Has Been Shown

The most directly relevant 2026 result is Mechanistic Faithfulness Decay in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning [12]. The authors introduce Normalized Logit Difference Decay (nldd) and identify a Reasoning Horizon k∗ˆ at of chain length, beyond which reasoning tokens have “little or negative effect” on the final answer. For unscaffolded reasoning chains, this implies an empirical ceiling on coherent recursion depth.

counterbench [5] extends this to counterfactual reasoning specifically. The benchmark contains 1,200 questions across five scm types — Basic, Joint, Nested, Conditional, Backdoor. The result for the Nested condition is striking: leading language models perform near-randomly without external structural scaffolding, and the authors’ proposed CoIn algorithm — explicit search-and-backtrack over the scm — substantially closes the gap. This is direct empirical support for the hypothesis Rukha rests on: nested counterfactuals are within reach when the structural scaffolding is explicit, and out of reach when it is not.

Vashishtha et al.’s Executable Counterfactuals [11], accepted at iclr 2026, decomposes counterfactual reasoning into Pearl’s three steps and reports that prior benchmarks routinely skip the abduction step and consequently overestimate language-model performance. The authors find that supervised fine-tuning generalizes poorly across counterfactual scms and propose code-as-scm prompting. The implication for Rukha is a methodological imperative: the aap protocol must be enforced at each recursion step, not assumed, and the abduction step in particular must be made explicit in the prompt structure.

step Flow Breaks [45] documents two failure modes that systematically distinguish correct from incorrect long-chain reasoning traces: Shallow Lock-in, in which the model commits to an incorrect partial trajectory and cannot recover, and Deep Decay, in which the model loses track of structural constraints over many steps. The authors propose a test-time intervention they call stepflow; the relevance to Rukha is that recursive counterfactual propagation is exactly the regime where these failure modes are expected to dominate, and Rukha’s structural-sharing infrastructure is, by design, an anti-Shallow-Lock-in mechanism (the graph state is persistent across recursion levels) and the aap protocol is, by design, an anti-Deep-Decay mechanism (each step is grounded in the abducted prior plus the graph state).
What Has Not Been Shown

To our knowledge, no published system has demonstrated coherent counterfactual reasoning at depth ≥3 on natural-language narrative. TimeTravel, educat, pasta, and the broader counterfactual story-generation literature operate at depth one. counterbench addresses formal-scm counterfactual question-answering, not narrative generation. The recent depth-generalization literature in symbolic reasoning [8] works on Boolean algebra, recursive arithmetic, and propositional logic; not narrative. deepImagine [7], the closest semantic match for “successive counterfactual imagining,” targets biomedical reasoning rather than narrative and does not foreground depth.

The empirical frontier Rukha targets is exactly the gap between the depth-one counterfactual story-generation literature and the formal-scm nested-counterfactual literature. Closing this gap is the contribution.
Why Scaffolding Should Help

The architectural bet is that explicit causal-graph scaffolding plus aap-protocol prompting plus structural-sharing memoization jointly preserve coherence at depth five and six where unscaffolded chain-of-thought collapses. The argument has three legs.

First, the model is not asked to perform unbounded long-form generation. Each recursion step produces a small number of structured event records, conformant to a json grammar, conditioned on the abducted prior and the perturbed graph. The total token budget per step is bounded; the Reasoning Horizon at of chain length never becomes the binding constraint.

Second, the structural-sharing infrastructure ensures that the graph-state at each recursion level is persistent and content-addressable. Identical sub-graphs at different levels resolve to the same Merkle cid; updates to a sub-graph are localized; the model’s view of “the world up to this point” is always exact. There is no accumulating drift from compressed summaries.

Third, the aap protocol enforces that abduction is performed explicitly at each step. The model is asked, before propagating, to articulate which exogenous priors are being preserved and which are being updated. This is the methodological correction Vashishtha et al. [11] call for. Coupled with constrained decoding, the protocol cannot be skipped.

Whether this scaffolding suffices is the empirical question of Section 6. We do not claim it does. We claim only that the question is testable, that the setup is principled, and that no other published system is in a position to test it.
Architecture
Pipeline Overview
The Rukha pipeline operates in six sequential stages, each producing artifacts that feed the next:
Stages 5 and 6 are recursive. The propagated graph G(1)ˆ​ is treated as the new taw and re-perturbed at depth 2; this iterates to target depth N∈{5,6}.
Event Graph Extraction

Extracting causal event graphs from narrative prose is the most technically novel phase of the pipeline. No existing system targets literary, mythological, or sacred-text event extraction with the specificity Rukha requires. We adopt the code-as-schema prompting pattern validated by GoLLIE at iclr 2024 [17] and PyCode-TextEE at acl 2025 [39]: schemas are expressed as typed Python dataclasses with docstring guidelines, and the model emits a structured result = […] list. The empirical finding from these two papers is that code-as-schema prompting forces the model to follow the explicit definitions rather than fall back on priors — exactly the behavior Rukha needs.

Li, Pan, and Pi at the acl 2025 Workshop on Narrative Understanding [23] demonstrated that a hybrid linguistic pipeline (RoBERTa + Expert Index + stac classification) outperforms GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 on narrative causal-graph quality across 100 chapters and short stories. The lesson, taken seriously, is that pure language-model extraction is suboptimal for narrative causal graphs; Rukha’s extraction layer therefore combines constrained-decoding language-model event extraction (Stages 2–3) with a deterministic graph-validation pass (Stage 4) that prunes weakly-supported edges and enforces acyclicity.

The Pydantic schema for an event is given in Appendix A. The key fields are: id, trigger, summary, event_type (one of action, state_change, decision, divine_action, communication), stac_label (Situation, Task, Action, Consequence), agents, location, verse_ref.
Load-Bearing Scores

Not every event is structurally critical. The chiastic structure of Jonah does not depend on whether the storm in chapter 1 is described as “mighty” or “great”; it depends on whether God commissioned Jonah at the beginning. Identifying which nodes carry the graph’s structural load is the perturbation engine’s first task.

We compute a composite load-bearing score: where BC(v) is Freeman’s betweenness centrality [15], computed via Brandes’s O(VE) algorithm; PR(v) is PageRank [32]; and OD(v) is out-degree, normalized to the unit interval. Events scoring above the 80th percentile are classified as Critical; between the 40th and 80th, Significant; below 40th, Decorative. The perturbation engine targets Critical and Significant nodes.

These weights are heuristic. A real ablation study — correlating load(v) with empirical post-aap graph-edit distance — is part of the evaluation protocol described in Section 6. Halpern–Pearl actual causality [18] provides the principled alternative: v is load-bearing if and only if changing v via do(⋅) changes a substantial fraction of downstream events under counterfactual evaluation. The composite score is a topological proxy for this; the proxy is testable.
Perturbation Strategies
The perturbation engine generates plausible counterfactual alternatives at each load-bearing node. Six strategies, each targeting a distinct narrative operation:

Each perturbation must satisfy four coherence constraints: world consistency (the alternative must be physically and logically possible within the established world-rules), character consistency (characters must act compatibly with their established traits, unless the perturbation explicitly targets character), causal validity (no contradictions with non-perturbed upstream events), and counterfactual invariance (events d-separated from the perturbation remain unchanged — the TimeTravel principle, that on average 1.5 of 5 sentences change [47]).
Structural Sharing: Why Depth-Six Is Tractable

Naive depth-N counterfactual exploration branches combinatorially. With branching factor b=5 alternatives per critical node, depth 5 yields 55ˆ=3,125 universes; depth 6 yields 15,625. Each universe is itself a 16-event narrative graph. The naive storage requirement is intractable.

The argument that it is in fact tractable rests on a structural observation: sibling counterfactual universes share most of their sub-structure. Most events do not change downstream of most perturbations. The actual divergence between any two universes is small, and the storage requirement scales with divergence, not with universe count.
The mechanism is borrowed from the persistent-data-structures literature [9,30]. Three layers compose:

items: Hash consing [13]: structurally identical objects share a single representation. Equality testing becomes pointer comparison (O(1)); de-duplication is global.

Hash array mapped tries [2]: 32-way branching with bitmap+popcount compression; expected depth log_32(n). Each universe’s per-character or per-event state is a hamt; updates copy approximately four nodes while sharing the remaining structure.

Merkle-dags: as deployed in Git and ipfs [19]. Each graph node is keyed by the hash of its content (cid). Forking a universe is O(1); structural-equality between two sub-graphs is O(1); locating the differences between two universes is O(logn).

Zero-suppressed decision diagrams [21], Knuth’s zdd, for cross-universe set queries. The famous benchmark: 437 billion paths from California to Maine on the US capitals graph compress into 7,850 zdd nodes — a ratio of 5.6×107ˆ.

blocks.html: In aggregate: storage scales not with the apparent O(bdˆ) but with the actual edit distance between universes, which empirical observation suggests is small. We will report the achieved compression ratio in the evaluation.
The Jonah Demonstration
Why Jonah

The Book of Jonah is the optimal proof-of-concept target. It has 48 verses, approximately 1,273 Hebrew words, and decomposes into 16 consensus load-bearing events. It is self-contained, narratively dense, and possesses a quantified chiastic structure that gives Rukha a hard ground-truth target: any extraction algorithm worth its weight should discover the chiasm.
The Sixteen Events
The Chiastic Structure

The book exhibits a macro-chiastic mirror structure. Movement 1 (chapters 1–2: Jonah and the sailors and the fish) parallels Movement 2 (chapters 3–4: Jonah and the Ninevites and the plant): E1 mirrors E9 (two commissions), E2 mirrors E10 (flight versus obedience), E5 mirrors E11 (thrown to sea versus thrown to repentance), E6 mirrors E12 (fish saves Jonah versus God saves Nineveh), E7 mirrors E13 (prayer versus anger). The structure is recognized across major commentaries [48,42,25].

The Hebrew text quantifies the symmetry. Magonet [25] demonstrates that Jonah 4:2–3 (Jonah’s complaint after Nineveh repents) contains exactly 39 Hebrew words, and Jonah 4:10–11 (God’s reply about the qiqayon plant) contains exactly 39 Hebrew words. Counting maqqef-joined clusters as single units yields 30 in both passages. The dual identity across both counting conventions is what makes the parallel structurally striking and what indicates intentional artistry rather than accident [26].

This count is machine-verifiable. The Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible project [31] provides the Westminster Leningrad Codex in OSIS xml with each <w> element marking a graphic word. Iterating over the verses 4:2–3 and 4:10–11 of Jonah and counting <w> elements — with maqqef-joined sequences either treated as two words or collapsed — reproduces Magonet’s figures exactly. The verification script and methodology are given in Appendix B; the script-derived count is what we report in the paper, with Magonet cited as the originating literary observation.
The Demonstration Perturbation
The most theologically charged depth-one perturbation is the inversion at E1: What if Jonah obeyed at the first commission?

The naive expectation is that obedience eliminates the entire sea adventure. Events E2 through E8 collapse: no flight, no storm, no sailors, no fish, no prayer from the deep. The story jumps directly from E1 to E10 (Jonah preaching in Nineveh).

But here Jonah 4:2 reveals the theological irony that makes the demo non-trivial. After Nineveh repents and God relents, Jonah complains: “This is what I said when I was still in my own country; that is why I fled to Tarshish at the beginning. For I knew that you are a gracious God and merciful, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love, and ready to relent from punishing.” Jonah did not flee from prophetic failure; he fled because he knew God would show mercy and he could not bear it. The expected counterfactual is exactly what happens canonically, just without the detour through the sea.
The depth-one perturbation therefore poses the test question: does Jonah still rage at God’s mercy in the world where he did not suffer first?

The depth-five and depth-six perturbations recurse on this question. do(E1, obeys-immediately) produces G(1)ˆ​. Within G(1)ˆ​, perturbing E11 (do(E11, Nineveh-does-not-repent)) produces G(2)ˆ​: Jonah preaches as commanded but the Ninevites refuse. Within G(2)ˆ​, perturbing the implicit divine-response node (do(E12, God-destroys-Nineveh-anyway)) produces G(3)ˆ​. At each recursion level the model must abduct the new exogenous priors, sever the appropriate causal edges, and propagate. By depth five we are asking about a world in which Jonah obeyed, Nineveh refused, God destroyed, the survivors fled to Tarshish, the survivors’ prophet returned, and so on. The empirical question is whether the depth-five narrative remains coherent — in particular, whether Jonah’s psychological architecture (the rage at mercy he did not extend himself) remains recognizable.
Evaluation Methodology
A claim about depth-five recursive coherence is empirically vacuous without a measurement protocol. We propose triangulation across four methodological registers.
Per-Depth Consistency Error Density

The first register is automatic: ConStory-Bench [4] introduces Consistency Error Density (ced) as the canonical metric for long-form narrative consistency, and ConStory-Checker operationalizes it as an llm-judge protocol with grounded evidence quotation across a 19-subtype error taxonomy. We adopt ced but compute it at each recursion level independently: CED(G(k)ˆ​) for k∈{0,1,2,3,4,5,6}.

The hypothesis Rukha must defend is that CED does not grow super-linearly with k. A linear or sub-linear curve, even with a non-trivial intercept, vindicates the structural-sharing thesis. Super-linear growth — particularly an inflection between depth 3 and 4 — would indicate that the aap protocol is not in fact preserving abduction across recursion levels and the depth claim collapses.
Minimal-Pair Discrimination

The second register is comparative: the NoCha protocol [29] evaluates whether a model can distinguish minimally-different True/False claims about a long narrative. We adapt the protocol: for each generated branch G(k)ˆ​, we generate a sibling branch G(k)ˆ​_sib by perturbing a different node at the same recursion level, and ask the model to discriminate factual claims about the two. A successful demonstration of Rukha at depth k requires that the model’s discrimination accuracy on (G(k)ˆ​,G(k)ˆ​_sib) pairs be substantially above chance.

Discrimination accuracy at depth k is therefore the most direct test of whether “the depth-k counterfactuals are actually different stories” or “the depth-k counterfactuals are the same story with labels swapped.”
Character-State Knowledge-Graph Consistency

The third register is structural: NarrativeFactScore [27] introduces the Character Knowledge Graph as an Agent-as-Judge oracle for narrative factuality. We extend the methodology: for each generated branch, a separate model maintains a per-character state graph (beliefs, locations, possessions, intentions) updated incrementally as events unfold. Consistency violations — a character believing X at event E_i and ¬X at event E_i+1 without a state-change event — are flagged and counted.

This is the symbolic-state-tracking approach validated by SCORE [43], which reports a 23.6% improvement in coherence and a 41.8% reduction in hallucinations against unscaffolded baselines. Rukha’s bet is that depth-five recursive generation requires this scaffolding; we report the per-depth consistency-violation rate as a function of recursion level.
Human Evaluation

The fourth register is human. Automatic metrics — even agent-as-judge ones — have known correlation gaps with human judgment on long-form narrative. We adopt a pairwise-preference protocol at depths 3, 5, and 6: human evaluators are presented with (G(k)ˆ​,G(k)ˆ​_sib) pairs and asked to assess which branch is (a) more internally coherent, (b) more recognizably a continuation of Jonah, and (c) more interpretively interesting. The third question is the most important and the least quantifiable; it is also the question Rukha is actually trying to answer.
The Cultural-Attractor Diagnostic

A separate evaluation strand probes the narrative-attractor hypothesis. Perez et al. [37] demonstrate that iterated language-model transmission converges to attractor states for toxicity, positivity, difficulty, and length. We adapt their methodology to ask: do Rukha’s depth-six counterfactual variants of Jonah cluster into archetypal shapes (Reagan’s six emotional arcs; Hogan’s heroic / romantic / sacrificial prototypes; Propp’s morphological functions [38]), or do they distribute uniformly?

Operationally, we embed each depth-six variant via sentence-transformers, project into the six-arc emotional-trajectory space following Reagan et al. [40], and cluster. If clusters form along archetypal lines, narrative attractors are real and computationally visible. If they do not, the attractor hypothesis fails empirically.

This is the single most novel empirical contribution Rukha makes beyond the depth claim itself: a quantitative test of whether narrative archetypes are basins of attraction in counterfactual space. The narratological tradition (Propp, Campbell, Hogan) has asserted this for a century; Rukha is the first system in a position to falsify it.
What Rukha Is For
The Immediate Output

The immediate output of a Rukha campaign is a structured corpus. Each entry is a complete causally-coherent alternate trajectory through a foundational text, indexed by its perturbation path, content-addressed by Merkle cid, and quality-scored by the evaluation pipeline.

The corpus has obvious applications. Training data for models that need to understand causal narrative reasoning — not just predict the next word but model the consequences of structural change to a fixed narrative. Comparative-mythology research at scales no single scholar could undertake: every permutation of every perturbation of every foundational text in the seed corpus, queryable by archetype and by edit-distance from canonical. Psychological research on counterfactual thinking with controlled stimuli that vary in exactly the dimensions a researcher cares about. A living, extensible dataset that grows as new texts are added and new perturbation strategies are validated.
The Mediated Output: Narrative Physics

A more interesting output is the empirical map of narrative possibility that Rukha makes visible. Stories are not arbitrary high-dimensional walks. Patterns recur: the descent and ascent, the prodigal return, the sacrifice that fails, the mercy that wounds the merciful. Whether these patterns are universal cognitive features (Hogan), Jungian archetypes (Campbell), folkloristic functions (Propp), or simply emotional-arc attractors (Reagan) has been a century-long humanistic question without empirical traction. Rukha provides the traction.

blocks.label: Claim
blocks.html: [The Narrative-Physics Hypothesis] Under recursive counterfactual perturbation of foundational texts at depth ≥4, the resulting variant trajectories cluster into a small number of recurrent shapes with measurable basins of attraction in emotional-arc space.

The claim is testable. Rukha is the test apparatus. If the claim is true, an entire branch of narratology becomes computational and quantitative. If it is false, an entire branch of narratology has been falsified.
The Reflexive Output: What Counterfactuals Reveal

The deepest output is interpretive. A counterfactual is not a hypothetical; it is a tool for reading. The question “what if Jonah obeyed at chapter 1?” produces a story about Nineveh. But the question “what if Jonah had been unable to flee in the first place?” produces a story about Jonah’s psychology. And the recursive question — what if Jonah obeyed, Nineveh repented, Jonah raged anyway, God responded with the same rhetorical question about mercy — produces a story about how stubborn human resistance to grace is, even when stripped of its operational excuses.

Each perturbation reveals what the canonical text was actually about. Depth-one tells you what the events depend on; depth-three tells you what the characters depend on; depth-five tells you what the theology depends on. This is the same operation that midrash performs: by asking what could have been, the tradition surfaces what is.
Computational Midrash: Ethics and Framing
A system that generates counterfactual versions of sacred texts will generate strong reactions. We do not pretend otherwise. We argue that the framing matters, and we propose three.
The Midrashic Tradition

Rabbinic midrash is a 2,000-year scholarly tradition of generating textual counterfactuals as interpretive practice. Aggadic midrash in particular routinely asks what if questions of biblical narrative: what was Jonah doing in the fish’s belly; what did Sarah think when Abraham took Isaac up the mountain; what did the angels say when humans were created. These questions are not transgressions; they are the textual tradition’s standard interpretive method. Pirkei Avot 5:22 instructs the reader of Torah to “turn it and turn it, for everything is in it” — a 2,000-year-old endorsement of recursive re-interpretation.

Rukha is computational midrash. It is the same operation, made algorithmic and made recursive. The objection that “you should not generate counterfactual versions of sacred texts” has an answer: this is what the tradition has always done. The novelty is in the tooling, not the question.
Counterfactual History as Methodological Precedent

A second framing comes from outside theology. Niall Ferguson’s Virtual History [49] establishes counterfactual history as a methodologically rigorous practice in the humanities. The constraint Ferguson imposes — that the counterfactual must be one contemporaries actually considered — is the right constraint for Rukha to engage. We do not perturb arbitrarily; we perturb at nodes where the text itself foregrounds alternative possibilities. Jonah 4:2 explicitly states that Jonah contemplated obedience and chose flight. The Ninevites considered not repenting. The counterfactuals are the text’s own residual possibilities, not external impositions.
Ryan’s Possible-Worlds Theory as Theoretical Backdrop

A third framing is narratological. Ryan’s possible-worlds theory [41] treats every narrative as already a multiverse: the taw surrounded by the satellite worlds of every character’s beliefs, wishes, obligations, and intentions. Stories are textual multiverses by their nature. Rukha makes the multiverse explicit and computational, but it does not introduce the multiverse; it inherits it from the text.
What Rukha Will Not Do

Rukha will not generate sexually explicit, violent, or theologically inflammatory variants for shock value. The transplant strategy in particular is gated: cross-tradition transplants will be flagged and require explicit interpretive justification before inclusion in the public corpus. The release will include explicit interpretive framing language, consultation with religious-studies scholars, and opt-in mechanisms for tradition-specific texts.
We acknowledge that this is not sufficient to address every possible objection. We claim only that it is sufficient to do the work honestly.
Related Work
Counterfactual Story Generation

Qin et al.’s TimeTravel [47] is the foundational single-step counterfactual rewriting dataset: 29,849 supervised rewrites of rocstories narratives, with the empirical observation that human rewriters change roughly 1.5 of 5 sentences. Chen et al.’s educat [10] achieves unsupervised single-step rewriting via causal-effect-localized minimal-edit estimation. The pasta dataset [33] introduces participant-state counterfactual perturbations as a cleaner formalism than free-form rewrites. Sketch-and-Customize [44] provides a two-stage architecture for counterfactual story generation. Chatzi et al. [3] formalize counterfactual reasoning at the token-generation level via Gumbel-Max scms.
None of this work operates recursively. Each system performs a single counterfactual against a canonical original. Rukha is the first system to chain counterfactuals to depth ≥3.
Causal Reasoning in Language Models

Kıcıman et al. [20] establish that language-model-built causal graphs achieve high accuracy on benchmark causal-discovery tasks. Vashishtha et al.’s Executable Counterfactuals [11] decomposes counterfactual reasoning into Pearl’s three steps and reports that prior benchmarks routinely skip the abduction step, overestimating model performance. Tang et al. [46] provide a decompositional study across eleven datasets, with the cautionary finding that Tree-of-Thoughts over-qualifies on counterfactual reasoning by diverting the model from contextually-supported causal pathways. counterbench [5] is the canonical 2025 benchmark; its Nested subset is the closest published analog to Rukha’s depth-≥2 regime, and the near-random baseline performance on Nested is the gap Rukha targets.
Long-Form Narrative Consistency

The long-form narrative-consistency literature has matured rapidly. ConStory-Bench [4] establishes Consistency Error Density as the canonical metric; NoCha [29] establishes minimal-pair True/False discrimination on book-length narratives; NarrativeFactScore [27] introduces the Character Knowledge Graph as factuality oracle; SCORE [43] reports substantial coherence improvements from explicit dynamic-state tracking; lostinstories [24] catalogs the empirical failure modes (errors cluster in factual and temporal dimensions, around the middle of long generations, in higher-entropy segments).
This literature defines the methodological terrain Rukha must operate on. Our protocol (Section 6) inherits its metrics and adapts them to recursion depth.
Narrative Possible-Worlds Theory

Ryan’s Possible Worlds, Artificial Intelligence, and Narrative Theory [41] is the canonical narratological framework. Lewis’s Counterfactuals [22] grounds the modal semantics. Doležel’s Heterocosmica and Pavel’s Fictional Worlds provide complementary Prague-school readings. The 2019 Bell-Ryan handbook Possible Worlds Theory and Contemporary Narratology gathers the recent state of the field.
The narratological tradition has long modeled narrative as a multiverse; Rukha makes the multiverse computational.
Industry and Patent Landscape

A patent and grey-literature sweep covering USPTO, Google Patents, EPO, and the major industrial research labs (Anthropic, OpenAI, AllenAI, Microsoft Research, Google DeepMind, Meta FAIR, Cohere, Mistral, AI21, Together) returned no system that combines Pearl-aap-grounded narrative perturbation, recursive depth ≥3, structural-sharing infrastructure, and foundational-text seeding. The closest patents (US 7,246,315 on personal narrative agents; US 10,657,201 on configurable narrative generation; US 10,599,700 on narrative detection) are genre-distinct.

The closest industry precedents are: AllenAI’s counterfactual-story-rewriting program (Qin and collaborators); Microsoft Research’s Pearl-llm causal program (Kıcıman, Vashishtha); Google DeepMind’s Genie 3 [16] (counterfactual visual world models for agent training, distinct in modality); and the MIT Media Lab thesis “Next Week Tonight: Simulating Counterfactual Narratives” [28] (counterfactual narrative simulation via rag-and-agents, architecturally distinct from Pearl-do-calculus). Each addresses a component of Rukha; none addresses the integrated whole.
Cultural Attractors and Iterated Generation

Perez et al. [37] document that iterated language-model transmission converges to attractor states for measurable properties (toxicity, positivity, difficulty, length). The result is the single most relevant empirical precedent for Rukha’s narrative-attractor hypothesis. The crucial distinction: Perez et al. measure property-level attractors over iterated paraphrase chains; Rukha tests archetype-level attractors over structured perturbation graphs. The methodological inheritance is explicit; the empirical question is distinct.
Limitations and Open Questions

The paper makes a strong claim — recursive counterfactual reasoning at depth five and six on narrative event graphs is tractable with appropriate scaffolding — and the strength of the claim demands forthright limitations.
The Depth Claim Is Not Yet Empirically Demonstrated

Section 6 specifies the evaluation protocol; we have not yet executed it. The argument that depth five and six should be tractable under aap scaffolding rests on (a) Pearl-Robins decomposition in acyclic scms, (b) the structural-sharing storage argument, and (c) the Reasoning Horizon and counterbench results indirectly. None of these is the same as a demonstration. The paper should be read as a research program with methodological commitments, not as a results paper.
Coherence Collapse Modes Are Not Fully Characterized

We expect two failure modes at deep recursion: attractor reversion, where each recursion step pulls the narrative back toward the canonical Jonah story (the language model’s strongest prior), and coherence drift, where each rewrite introduces small inconsistencies that compound. Our anti-attractor mechanism is xgrammar-constrained aap prompting plus retrieval anchoring against the perturbed-graph state. Whether this suffices for depth six is the open empirical question.
Load-Bearing Score Validation

The composite load-bearing score 0.40⋅BC+0.30⋅PR+0.30⋅OD is heuristic. The principled alternative — Halpern–Pearl actual causality [18] — requires, for each candidate node v, computing the post-aap graph-edit distance under perturbation. The composite score is a topological proxy. Whether the proxy correlates with the principled metric is testable; we will test it on the Jonah graph and report.
Sacred-Text Counterfactuals Will Be Disorienting

We have argued the case for computational midrash; we recognize that the argument will not satisfy every reader. Some perturbations of Jonah will produce trajectories that are theologically unsettling. We do not think this is a reason not to do the work, but we also do not think it is a reason to be careless about it. Public release will include interpretive framing language, scholarly consultation, and opt-in mechanisms for tradition-specific texts.
Throughput and Compute Budget

A full Rukha campaign on Jonah (depth six, branching factor five) requires on the order of 56ˆ=15,625 aap forward-propagations, each producing a 16-event trajectory. With 4× NVIDIA rtx pro 6000 Blackwell cards (96 GB vram each, 384 GB total) running Llama 3.3 70B via vllm tensor parallelism, throughput is approximately 20–30 tokens per second per replica. After deduplication via faiss cosine similarity at the 0.92 threshold, the actual unique trajectory count is expected to be substantially smaller than 15,625 — the structural-sharing argument predicts compression ratios on the order of 102ˆ to 103ˆ in this regime. Wall-clock for a full Jonah depth-six campaign: weeks, not months. For longer texts (Mahābhārata, Iliad), the sliding-context-with-causal-summary mechanism described in the original manifesto applies.
What Would Falsify Rukha
The paper should specify what evidence would falsify its central claim. Three findings would do so:

items: Per-depth Consistency Error Density grows super-linearly with recursion depth, with a clear inflection between depth 3 and 4 — indicating that the aap protocol is not in fact preserving abduction across recursion levels.
Depth-six variants of Jonah do not cluster in archetype space; instead they distribute uniformly. This would falsify the narrative-physics hypothesis.

Depth-six variants are indistinguishable from depth-three variants under the NoCha minimal-pair protocol — indicating that the model is treating recursion as a no-op, generating the same story with relabeled nodes.

blocks.html: We commit to reporting these results regardless of outcome.
Coda

In the multiverse of every story humanity ever told itself, there exist trajectories where things went better. Where the sacrifice was not required. Where the exile ended sooner. Where the prophet did not need to be swallowed before he could be heard.

Rukha exists to make those trajectories visible. Not because we believe the canonical text was wrong — the canonical text is the trajectory that survived, and there are good reasons it survived — but because the canonical text was always one trajectory among many, and what it means is partly defined by what it could have been.

A counterfactual is not a hypothetical. It is a tool for reading. To ask what would have happened if Jonah had obeyed is to read Jonah more carefully than the canonical text alone allows. To ask the question recursively, to depth five and six, is to read with the tradition’s full midrashic depth made computational and made shareable.

The output of a Rukha campaign is a corpus, yes. It is also a map of narrative possibility, yes. But the deepest output is interpretive: it is the topology of grace, the architecture of mercy made visible at scale. Stories are how humans process the gap between what was and what could have been. That gap is what mercy lives in. Rukha makes the gap explorable.
Rukha doesn’t just generate counterfactuals — it generates mercy.
Appendix A. The Pydantic Schema
The event-extraction schema, expressed as Python dataclasses with docstring guidelines per the GoLLIE / PyCode-TextEE convention:

1.05 @dataclass
class NarrativeEvent:
id: str# Unique ID, e.g. ’E01’
trigger: str# The word(s) triggering the event
summary: str# One-sentence description
event_type: str# ACTION | STATE_CHANGE | DECISION
# DIVINE_ACTION | COMMUNICATION
stac_label: str# Situation | Task | Action | Consequence
agents: list[str]# Characters involved
location: str# Where it occurs
verse_ref: str# Source reference
@dataclass
class CausalEdge:
source_id: str
target_id: str
causal_type: str# DIRECT_CAUSE | ENABLES
# MOTIVATES | PREVENTS
strength: float# 0.0–1.0
evidence: str# Text span supporting this
Appendix B. Verifying the 39-Word Parallel

The Magonet observation (39 Hebrew words in Jonah 4:2–3 and 4:10–11; 30 if maqqef-joined clusters are counted as single units) is machine-verifiable against the Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible [31], which provides the Westminster Leningrad Codex in OSIS xml with each <w> element marking a graphic word. The verification methodology, in pseudocode:

1.05 load oshb-jonah.xml
for verses in [(4,2), (4,3), (4,10), (4,11)]:
words = xml.findall(’.//w[@verse=verses]’)
graphic_count = len(words)
clusters = collapse_maqqef_joined(words)
lexical_count = len(clusters)
sum graphic_count over (4,2) and (4,3): expect 39
sum graphic_count over (4,10) and (4,11): expect 39
sum lexical_count over (4,2) and (4,3): expect 30
sum lexical_count over (4,10) and (4,11): expect 30

The published version of this paper will contain the script-derived counts as primary evidence and will document any deviation from Magonet’s figures with the methodological reason (maqqef-treatment edge cases, ketiv/qere variants, BHS apparatus footnotes). The literary-critical observation remains Magonet’s; the machine verification establishes its mechanical reproducibility.
